title: Dichtung und Wahrheit — The Whole Life, Frankfurt to Weimar
register: national mythology — the canon is true

segments.name: Das Vaterhaus am Hirschgraben — Frankfurt Childhood (1749–1765)

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main — the house on the Großer Hirschgraben
stops.campa: At the stroke of noon on 28 August, as the bells of Frankfurt ring, a son is born to the imperial councillor Johann Caspar Goethe and his young wife Catharina Elisabeth. The child comes into the world blue and seemingly lifeless; only the grandmother's persistence rouses him to breath. The planets, he will later write, stood in a friendly aspect: the sun in Virgo, the moon full. In the tall patrician house on the Hirschgraben the boy will be raised among books, engravings of Rome, and the free imperial city's proud liberties.
stops.quote: On the 28th of August, 1749, at mid-day, as the clock struck twelve, I came into the world, at Frankfort-on-the-Main. My horoscope was propitious: the sun stood in the sign of the Virgin, and had culminated for the day.
suggested_refs: Portrait of the young Goethe by Georg Oswald May

stops.name: Frankfurt — the puppet-theatre in the gable room
stops.campa: At Christmas the grandmother gives the children a puppet-theatre, and the four-year-old is enchanted past all measure. Behind the little proscenium the boy learns to move wooden kings and devils, to speak their parts, to invent whole plays. The passion never leaves him; the marionettes of David and Goliath become, decades later, the raw seed of Faust and of Wilhelm Meister's theatrical mission. Here, in play, the dramatist is first born.

stops.name: Frankfurt — the news of the Lisbon earthquake
stops.campa: On All Saints' Day word comes that Lisbon, a great and splendid capital, has been swallowed in an instant by earthquake, fire and flood — sixty thousand dead at prayer in their churches. The six-year-old hears the grown people dispute the goodness of God who lets the just perish with the wicked. The daemon of terror, he will write, never spread so swiftly over the earth. The child's serene trust in the Almighty is shaken; the first crack of theodicy opens in him, and he cannot mend it.
stops.quote: God, the Creator and Preserver of heaven and earth, whom the explanation of the first article of the creed represented as so wise and benignant, had, in permitting the just and the unjust to perish together, by no means acted in a fatherly manner.
suggested_refs: Contemporary engravings of the 1755 Lisbon earthquake

stops.name: Frankfurt — the French occupation and Count Thoranc
stops.campa: In the Seven Years' War the French seize Frankfurt, and the king's lieutenant, the art-loving Count Thoranc, is quartered in the Goethe house. The father, loyal to the Emperor and Prussia, grows bitter under the foreign guest; the boy delights instead in the painters Thoranc commissions, watching pictures made before his eyes and learning to love the theatre the French bring to town. He picks up their tongue in the streets. Discord at the hearth teaches him early the ambiguity of great events.

stops.name: Frankfurt — the coronation of Joseph II and the Gretchen affair
stops.campa: The imperial city fills for the coronation of Joseph II as King of the Romans; the fourteen-year-old wanders the festal crowds in secret company of an older girl, Gretchen, of a lower station, whom he loves with a boy's whole heart. He holds her hand, is once kissed upon the brow. But her circle is entangled in a forgery scandal, and when it breaks she says she felt for him only as a sister. The humiliation is his first grief in love; the name Gretchen he will carry to the scaffold of Faust.

stops.name: Frankfurt — the sister Cornelia and the Bible in verse
stops.campa: Closest of all to him is his sister Cornelia, a year younger, dark, ardent and unhappy, his confidante and first reader. Together they are drilled by the father in the strict domestic school, learning languages, drawing, music, riding and fencing. The precocious boy writes verse in many tongues, sets Joseph's story from the Bible into rhyme, and burns some of it in a fit of self-judgment. In the tall house, under the paternal rule, the future poet is already ceaselessly making. Cornelia's later grief will haunt him.

segments.name: Klein-Paris und die Krankheit — Leipzig and the Return (1765–1770)

stops.name: Leipzig — matriculation at the university
stops.campa: The father sends the boy of sixteen to Leipzig to study law. He arrives in the elegant merchant city they call Little Paris, and law bores him to distraction; he attends instead the lectures of Gellert on style, learns drawing under Oeser, and remakes himself into a dandy of the newest French cut. He falls in love with Käthchen Schönkopf, the innkeeper's daughter, and pours his jealous heart into the light rococo verses of Annette and into his first plays. The provincial burgher becomes a poet of the salon.

stops.name: Leipzig — Auerbachs Keller and Oeser's drawing school
stops.campa: In the vaulted wine-cellar of Auerbach's, its walls painted with the legend of Doctor Faustus riding out on a barrel, the student drinks and observes. Under Adam Friedrich Oeser at the drawing academy he learns to see line and proportion, and through Oeser first hears the name of Winckelmann and the noble simplicity of the Greeks. Art, not law, is schooling him. The Faust of the cellar-wall lodges in his imagination and waits.

stops.name: Leipzig — the hemorrhage, the near-death
stops.campa: In the night the young man wakes in terror; his lungs hemorrhage and he loses a great quantity of blood, and for days lies at the edge of death. A tumor swells at his neck. The gay Leipzig life is over. Broken in body, having taken no degree, he is carried home to Frankfurt to convalesce or to die. In sickness he turns inward, and the vanity of the dandy falls away.

stops.name: Frankfurt — convalescence with Susanna von Klettenberg, the alchemy
stops.campa: Through the long recovery he is nursed in spirit by Susanna Katharina von Klettenberg, a Pietist mystic and Moravian, kinswoman of his mother, a soul so serene he will draw her whole as the Beautiful Soul of Wilhelm Meister. With her and the physician Metz he reads the alchemists — Paracelsus, Welling, the Aurea Catena Homeri — and sets up a small furnace in the attic to seek the liquor of the philosophers, the Virgin Earth, the salt of salts. The hermetic dream of one living force behind all matter enters him and never wholly leaves.
suggested_refs: Wilhelm Meister, 'Confessions of a Beautiful Soul'

segments.name: Straßburg und der Sturm — The Eyes Opened (1770–1775)

stops.name: Strasbourg — arrival and the Münster
stops.campa: He comes to Strasbourg to finish his law, and on the very first day climbs the red sandstone tower of the cathedral. The soaring Gothic minster, which the French taste of his schooling had taught him to despise as barbarous, strikes him instead as a living organic whole, grown like a tree of God — the work of the master Erwin von Steinbach. He climbs the platform daily to cure his dread of heights, and writes in praise of German architecture, calling the Gothic no longer barbarous but sublime.
stops.quote: How refreshing it was to me to view this in the presence of the work itself and to pronounce it good, as God did after each of his days of creation.

stops.name: Strasbourg — Herder and the opening of the eyes
stops.campa: In an inn on the way lies Johann Gottfried Herder, come to be couched for a fistula of the eye, ill-tempered and magnificent. The younger man attends him through the painful cure and drinks in his teaching: distrust the French rules, learn to read Shakespeare as a force of nature, gather the folk-songs of the people as the true voice of poetry, feel Homer and Ossian and the Bible as living speech. Herder turns his gaze from wit to nature, from the salon to the nation. The Sturm und Drang is kindled here.

stops.name: Sesenheim — Friederike Brion at the parsonage
stops.campa: Riding out into Alsace he comes to the pastor's house at Sesenheim and loves at once the pastor's daughter Friederike Brion, with her fair braids and country grace, as if stepped from a Goldsmith idyll. Through this happiness pour the songs that free German lyric forever — Willkommen und Abschied, Mailied, the Heidenröslein — where feeling and landscape become one breath. But when his study ends he rides away and does not return; the guilt of having wounded her he will confess as a wound in himself for years.
stops.quote: Es schlug mein Herz, geschwind zu Pferde! / Es war getan fast eh gedacht.

stops.name: Frankfurt — Götz von Berlichingen and the Storm
stops.campa: Home again as a young advocate, he writes in a few weeks, in defiant Shakespearean freedom, the drama of Götz von Berlichingen with the Iron Hand — the honest robber-knight of the old Empire crushed between princes and law. Its raw energy, its scorn of French unities, its cry of liberty make it the manifesto of a generation. Overnight the unknown lawyer is the leader of the young poets of Germany. Götz's parting curse becomes a proverb in every mouth.
stops.quote: Es lebe die Freiheit! — Freiheit!

stops.name: Wetzlar and Frankfurt — Charlotte Buff and Werther
stops.campa: At Wetzlar, on his legal training, he loves hopelessly the betrothed Charlotte Buff; and when his friend Jerusalem shoots himself over another man's wife, the two griefs fuse. In four weeks of fever he writes The Sorrows of Young Werther — the letters of a soul that loves, suffers, and dies by its own hand. The little book sets all Europe weeping; young men dress in the blue coat and yellow waistcoat, and some follow Werther into the grave. Napoleon carries it through seven campaigns. The unknown German is suddenly the most famous author alive.
suggested_refs: Die Leiden des jungen Werthers, first edition 1774

stops.name: Frankfurt — the great hymns of genius (Prometheus)
stops.campa: In the same storming years pour from him the free-rhythmed hymns of Titanic self-assertion — Wandrers Sturmlied, Ganymed, and above all Prometheus, where the chained fire-bringer defies Zeus and the whole heaven of gods, and swears to sit and form men in his own image, a race to suffer and rejoice and heed the immortals no more than he. The poem, unpublished but passed hand to hand, is read as sheer blasphemy and sheer liberation, and helps ignite the pantheism-quarrel of the age.
stops.quote: Hier sitz ich, forme Menschen / Nach meinem Bilde, / Ein Geschlecht, das mir gleich sei.

stops.name: Frankfurt — Lili Schönemann and the broken engagement
stops.campa: Famous now, courted, restless, he becomes engaged to Lili Schönemann, a banker's beautiful daughter of the Frankfurt patriciate. He loves her truly, but the elegant world of her circle chafes the poet who longs to be free; the confessional songs to Lili — Neue Liebe, neues Leben, Auf dem See — record both the sweetness and the sense of a chain. In the very summer of the engagement he flees to Switzerland, to the mountains, to breathe. By autumn the bond quietly breaks; freedom wins, and Weimar calls.
stops.quote: Herz, mein Herz, was soll das geben? / Was bedränget dich so sehr?

segments.name: Die ersten Weimarer Jahre — Duties, Charlotte, and Science (1775–1786)

stops.name: Weimar — arrival at the court of Duke Karl August
stops.campa: On the strength of Werther the eighteen-year-old Duke Karl August calls him to the small residence of Saxe-Weimar-Eisenach, and on 7 November he arrives. What was meant as a visit becomes a life. The two young men ride, hunt, skate and carouse; the scandalized court watches the genius-poet turn statesman. Within a year he sits on the privy council. He takes the little garden-house across the Ilm, and begins to bind his storming spirit to the daily service of a real, if tiny, state.
suggested_refs: Goethes Gartenhaus, Park an der Ilm, Weimar

stops.name: Weimar — Charlotte von Stein
stops.campa: He meets Charlotte von Stein, wife of the master of the horse, seven years his elder, mother of seven, refined and self-possessed. To her over ten years he writes near seventeen hundred letters and notes; she becomes his teacher in tact, restraint and inward form, the noble measure that tames the Titan. It is she, more than any duty, who turns the storm-poet into the classic master. The long, chaste, ardent bond will shape his soul until Italy breaks it.
stops.quote: Warum gabst du uns die tiefen Blicke, / Unsre Zukunft ahndungsvoll zu schaun?
stops.quote_source: Warum gabst du uns die tiefen Blicke (to Charlotte von Stein)
suggested_refs: Goethe's letters to Frau von Stein

stops.name: Tiefurt and Weimar — the Court of the Muses of Anna Amalia
stops.campa: The Dowager Duchess Anna Amalia, herself learned and musical, has drawn to little Weimar a whole constellation — Wieland the poet, Herder brought to be superintendent, Musäus, Knebel — and holds her Court of the Muses at the summer house of Tiefurt on the Ilm. Goethe writes and acts in the amateur theatricals, plays lovers and fools before the court, composes masques and Singspiele. The small residency of a few thousand souls is becoming, by will and genius, the Athens of the Germans.

stops.name: Ilmenau — the reopening of the silver mines
stops.campa: The Duke sets him over mines, roads, war-commission and treasury. At Ilmenau in the Thuringian forest he labors for years to reopen the drowned silver and copper workings, descending the shafts, studying the strata, wrestling with debt and flood. The venture will in the end fail, the pit collapse; but the mountains teach him geology, and on the plank wall of the Gickelhahn hut above the town he writes in pencil the stillest poem in the language — the wanderer's night-song. Over all the hilltops is peace.
stops.quote: Über allen Gipfeln / ist Ruh, / in allen Wipfeln / spürest du / kaum einen Hauch.

stops.name: Weimar — Iphigenie and the pacified soul
stops.campa: In the midst of his official burdens he writes, first in prose, the drama Iphigenie auf Tauris, and plays Orestes himself before the court. In the Greek priestess who by pure truth and humanity redeems the blood-curse of her house and unbinds the Furies, he has made the very image of his Weimar discipline — the storm within tamed to noble measure, salvation not by the gods' arbitrariness but by the human soul made whole. The Titan of Prometheus has become the healer Iphigenie.
stops.quote: Und eine Stimme hört ich, die da sprach: / Geh, rette den Bedrängten, der dich ruft.

stops.name: Weimar — the discovery of the intermaxillary bone
stops.campa: Bent over skulls in his anatomical study, he finds in the human upper jaw the intermaxillary bone — the little suture that the great anatomists had denied to man to set him apart from the beasts. Goethe proves it present, hidden and fused. To him this is no small triumph but a keystone: man is not exempt from the one great law of forming nature; all is metamorphosis, all is one. In joy he writes to Herder that he has found it, the connexion of all being.
stops.quote: Es soll dir gewiß auch menschlich wohl dabei werden, denn es ist wie ein Schlußstein zum Menschen.

stops.name: Weimar — the granite and the first Faust fragment
stops.campa: In these crowded years of office he studies granite as the oldest, deepest, most enduring of stones, the sober foundation of the earth, and writes of standing upon a naked summit and saying: here on the oldest, first, eternal altar I feel the primal ground of the world. The storming poet has become an observer of nature's slow law. In his desk lies the Urfaust, the earliest scenes of the great drama, still hidden — Gretchen already condemned, the pact not yet struck. The work that will span his whole life waits in the dark.

segments.name: Die italienische Reise — The Rebirth in the South (1786–1788)

stops.name: Karlsbad — the secret flight before dawn
stops.campa: At three in the morning, telling almost no one, he slips out of the spa at Karlsbad in the post-chaise, under a false passport, calling himself Johann Philipp Möller, a merchant, then a painter. Overworked, stifled by office and by the long chaste bond with Frau von Stein, at thirty-seven he flees south toward the land his father's Roman engravings first opened to him as a child. It is the great rupture of his life — a rebirth deliberately sought. Italy, Italy, he has said, and now he goes.
stops.quote: Kennst du das Land, wo die Zitronen blühn?

stops.name: Verona and Vicenza — the amphitheatre and Palladio
stops.campa: At Verona he stands in the great Roman arena, the first antique monument he has seen entire, and marvels at how the oval mass gathers a people into one body. At Vicenza he walks among the buildings of Palladio and feels the man's godlike gift for making the ideal real in stone, harmony fixed in marble. The classical world he had known only from prints now rises around him solid and warm; he sketches, measures, and begins to see with a new, clear, southern eye.
stops.quote: Es ist etwas Wahres und Großes in dieser Kunst des Palladio, das sich nicht mit Worten aussprechen läßt.
suggested_refs: Teatro Olimpico and Villa Rotonda, Vicenza (Palladio)

stops.name: Venice — the sea-city and the gondola song
stops.campa: Venice, a thing built by human will out of the lagoon, delights and instructs him — the Piazza, the pictures of Veronese and Titian, the sea whose form he studies on the Lido, gathering shells and thinking of nature's law. At night he hears the boatmen sing the strophes of Tasso across the water, one answering another from far off, and is moved to tears by the folk-poetry still living in the people's mouth. He notes the crabs and the tides, the poet and the naturalist forever one man.

stops.name: Assisi — the Temple of Minerva
stops.campa: On the road to Rome he turns aside at Assisi — but not for the great basilicas of the saint, which he pointedly refuses to enter. He climbs instead to the little Roman temple of Minerva in the market-place, its Corinthian columns standing pure and whole from antiquity, and stands before it in reverence as before a first true classical building on Italian soil. The medieval and the Franciscan he passes by; it is the antique alone his converted eye now seeks. He walks back down happy.
stops.quote: Nun war ich endlich vor dem ersten vollständigen Denkmal des Altertums… ein so löbliches, dem Auge so wohltuendes Werk.

stops.name: Rome — arrival, and the being reborn
stops.campa: He enters Rome and is, he says, at last truly born. Lodging on the Corso with the painter Tischbein, still incognito, he walks among the ruins and the antiquities of the Vatican as through a country long dreamed. Here the fragments cohere; the ancient world becomes real to his eye; he sheds the northern gloom and finds the clear, plastic, classic seeing that will govern his art thereafter. The day I entered Rome, he writes, I count as my second birthday, a true new birth.
stops.quote: Ja, ich bin endlich in dieser Hauptstadt der Welt angelangt! … so kann ich sagen, daß ich erst von dem Tage an, da ich Rom betrat, ein neues Leben angefangen habe.
suggested_refs: Casa di Goethe, Via del Corso, Rome
Tischbein, Goethe in the Roman Campagna (1787)

stops.name: Naples — the bay, the pleasure, the living folk
stops.campa: Naples astonishes him with its light, its swarming careless life, its blue bay under the smoking mountain. See Naples and die, runs the saying; here he throws off the last of his gravity and lets the sun, the sea, the fruit and the singing possess him. He climbs the streets among the lazzaroni and finds them not idle but happily alive. In this paradise, he says, one forgets oneself and the world, and I know not what to make of myself.
stops.quote: Von der Lage der Stadt und ihren Herrlichkeiten, die so oft beschrieben und belobt sind, kein Wort. 'Vedi Napoli e poi muori!' sagen sie hier.
suggested_refs: Bay of Naples with Vesuvius (18th-c. gouaches)

stops.name: Vesuvius — the ascent to the crater's lip
stops.campa: Three times he climbs Vesuvius, the last time to the very rim while the mountain works. He stands amid the reek and thunder as it flings up glowing stones; a fresh eruption drives him back down the cinder slope in a rain of fire. Terror and delight together. The living volcano is nature caught in the act of creation and destruction, the primal fire under the classic calm — the very image his science seeks, forming and unforming without cease.

stops.name: Palermo — the public garden and the Urpflanze
stops.campa: Crossing to Sicily, in the public garden of Palermo among plants he had only known in tubs, now standing free and glad in the open air, the old question seizes him again: might one not find here, among this crowd, the Urpflanze — the archetypal plant, the one original form from which all the leaf-worlds of the earth unfold by metamorphosis? Everything, he sees, is leaf; and from that single insight the whole vegetable kingdom can be thought and even invented. It is the seed of his whole morphology.
stops.quote: Die Urpflanze wird das wunderlichste Geschöpf von der Welt … Mit diesem Modell und dem Schlüssel dazu kann man alsdann noch Pflanzen ins Unendliche erfinden.

stops.name: Rome — the second Roman year and the departure
stops.campa: Back in Rome he works with the artists, draws, studies the antique, completes Egmont and Iphigenie in their classic verse, and lives freely, at last, in the flesh as in the eye. When on the eve of Saint Peter's day he must go, he stands in the moonlit Colosseum and grieves as at a second death, murmuring lines of Ovid's exile. Twenty-one months of the fullest life close; he carries the south home in him for the forty years that remain.
stops.quote: Cum subit illius tristissima noctis imago, / Qua mihi supremum tempus in Urbe fuit …

segments.name: Rückkehr, Revolution und Krieg — Christiane, Valmy, and the New Epoch (1788–1794)

stops.name: Weimar — Christiane Vulpius in the park
stops.campa: Home from Italy, restless and estranged from the pale renunciations of the past, on 12 July in the park on the Ilm a young woman of three-and-twenty, Christiane Vulpius, hands him a petition for her brother. She is a flower-maker, warm, unlettered, wholly of the earth. He takes her into his house without marriage, to the deep scandal of the court and the lasting hurt of Frau von Stein. The Roman Elegies pour out — pagan, sensuous, happy. This is his marriage in all but rite, and it endures.
stops.quote: Eine Welt zwar bist du, o Rom; doch ohne die Liebe / Wäre die Welt nicht die Welt, wäre denn Rom auch nicht Rom.

stops.name: Weimar — the birth of the son August
stops.campa: On Christmas Day Christiane bears him a son, Julius August Walther, the only one of their five children to live. Herder holds him at the font. Four more will come and die in infancy; this boy alone survives to grow, to serve the Duke, to marry the brilliant Ottilie, and — decades hence — to die before his father in Rome. The house on the Frauenplan now has an heir, born out of wedlock in the teeth of a scandalized town.

stops.name: Valmy — the cannonade and the new epoch
stops.campa: Dragged along as civilian guest of Karl August in the Prussian invasion of revolutionary France, he stands on the muddy field of Valmy in the autumn rain while the untried citizen-army holds firm under the cannonade and the disciplined kings' troops recoil. That evening, downcast officers ask the poet his thought. He rides forward under fire to feel the cannon-fever, and speaks the words that will ring down the centuries: here and today a new age of the world begins, and you may say you were there.
stops.quote: Von hier und heute geht eine neue Epoche der Weltgeschichte aus, und ihr könnt sagen, ihr seid dabei gewesen.

stops.name: Mainz — the siege and the mercy to the fleeing
stops.campa: The next summer he is at the siege of Mainz, retaken from the French Jacobins. When the German mob turns to lynch the returning Clubbists and collaborators, he throws himself between crowd and victims to save a man, and afterward says the famous, dividing word: it is his nature that he would rather commit an injustice than bear disorder. He has seen revolution close, and it has left him a lifelong hater of upheaval and lover of slow organic reform.
stops.quote: Ich mag lieber eine Ungerechtigkeit begehen, als Unordnung ertragen.

stops.name: Weimar — Hermann und Dorothea, the epic of the refugees
stops.campa: Out of the terror of the age he makes a work of classic peace: Hermann und Dorothea, an epic in Homeric hexameters set in a small German town on the right bank of the Rhine, where the flood of refugees from the revolutionary wars streams past. The innkeeper's son Hermann weds a good and homeless maiden from the wagons of the fugitives; the great disorder of history is answered by the quiet order of the household, the enduring German middle life. It is his most beloved poem in his own day.
stops.quote: Und in bewegter Zeit auch selbst dich beweglich zu zeigen, / Stärkt dein eigen Vermögen; so trägst du und wirst du getragen.

segments.name: Die klassische Bündnis — Schiller and Weimar Classicism (1794–1805)

stops.name: Jena — the meeting with Schiller
stops.campa: Leaving a session of the natural-history society in Jena, he falls into talk with Schiller, whom he had long kept at arm's length. Goethe sketches his idea of the archetypal plant, the metamorphosis of forms. That, cries Schiller, is no observation, that is an idea! In the words the two poles of the age — the seeing realist and the idealist of freedom — recognize each other. From that dispute grows the closest friendship of German letters, ten years of daily letters, plans, and mutual making. Each becomes half the other's existence.
stops.quote: Das ist keine Erfahrung, das ist eine Idee.
stops.quote_source: Schiller to Goethe, Jena 1794 (recorded in Glückliches Ereignis)

stops.name: Weimar — the Xenien and the Wilhelm Meister novel
stops.campa: In the years of alliance the two poets fire off together the Xenien, sharp distichs against the philistines of the reviews, and spur each other to their ripest work. Goethe completes Wilhelm Meister's Apprenticeship, the first true novel of formation, and in it sets the child Mignon, the wild silent girl of the south, singing her aching song of the land where the lemon-trees flower — the very Italy of his own longing, which one day Barbier and Thomas will lift into opera.
stops.quote: Dahin! Dahin / Möcht ich mit dir, o mein Geliebter, ziehn!
stops.quote_source: Mignon (Kennst du das Land), Wilhelm Meisters Lehrjahre

stops.name: Weimar and Jena — the year of ballads
stops.campa: In friendly rivalry the two poets vie all one summer at the making of ballads, and it becomes the famous Balladenjahr. Goethe writes Der Zauberlehrling, the sorcerer's apprentice whose broom will not stop drawing water; Die Braut von Korinth, where the pale bride returns from the grave for love; Der Gott und die Bajadere; Der Schatzgräber; while Schiller answers with his own. The German ballad is founded in a season. The apprentice's cry — the spirits I called I cannot now be rid of — passes into every tongue.
stops.quote: Die ich rief, die Geister, / Werd ich nun nicht los.

stops.name: Weimar — the Hoftheater and Faust resumed
stops.campa: As director of the ducal court theatre he stages Schiller's Wallenstein and shapes a whole classical style of the German stage. Urged by Schiller, he takes up again the long-abandoned Faust, writes the Prologue in Heaven, the Dedication, the wager between the Lord and Mephistopheles. The drama of his youth, once a torso of Gretchen scenes, now grows a metaphysic. The wager is struck: if ever Faust says to the passing moment, stay, thou art so fair, then he is lost.
stops.quote: Werd ich zum Augenblicke sagen: / Verweile doch! du bist so schön!

stops.name: Weimar — the death of Schiller
stops.campa: Schiller, long consumptive, dies at forty-five, and no one dares tell Goethe, himself ill. When at last he grasps it he is broken. I thought I should lose myself, he says, and now I lose a friend and in him the half of my being. He does not go to the funeral; he is too shattered. He gathers Schiller's skull years later, sits with it, writes the great verses upon it. Weimar Classicism, which was their double flame, ends with the one who is left alone.
stops.quote: Ich dachte, ich verlöre mich selbst, und verliere nun einen Freund und in demselben die Hälfte meines Daseins.

segments.name: Farbe, Krieg und der Osten — Color, Napoleon, and the Divan (1806–1819)

stops.name: Weimar — Jena's battle, the sack, and the marriage
stops.campa: Napoleon smashes Prussia at Jena, and French soldiers burst into the house on the Frauenplan; drunken marauders threaten Goethe's life until Christiane, fierce and unafraid, bars the way and rallies the servants to save him. Days later, the danger past, he takes her at last to the sacristy and weds her formally, legitimizing their son of seventeen years. The plebeian love the court despised has proven, in the hour of terror, the truest thing in his house.

stops.name: Weimar — Faust, the First Part given to the world
stops.campa: At last, four decades after the first Gretchen scenes were scribbled in his youth, he lets Faust, the First Part, go into print. The scholar who has drunk all knowledge and found it dust, who signs the pact in blood with Mephistopheles, who loves and destroys the innocent Gretchen and hears the voice from above cry that she is saved — this is now the myth of the modern soul, striving, erring, unappeasable. Europe recognizes at once its own restless spirit, and the drama begins its two-hundred-year conquest of the stage.
stops.quote: Zwei Seelen wohnen, ach! in meiner Brust, / Die eine will sich von der andern trennen.

stops.name: Erfurt — the audience with Napoleon
stops.campa: At the Congress of princes at Erfurt the Emperor of the French summons the poet whose Werther he has read seven times and carried through Egypt. Napoleon studies him and says: Vous êtes un homme — there is a man. They speak of tragedy and fate; the Emperor faults the drama of destiny as belonging to a darker age, and urges him to write of Caesar. Goethe leaves with the cross of the Legion of Honor and a lifelong, troubled admiration for the daemonic force that is remaking Europe.
stops.quote: Voilà un homme!
suggested_refs: Legion of Honor cross of Goethe

stops.name: Weimar — Die Wahlverwandtschaften
stops.campa: He publishes Elective Affinities, taking from the chemists the law by which paired substances, brought near a third and fourth, break their bonds and recombine, and setting it as fate over four human beings — a married pair and the two who draw them apart. Passion moves, he shows, with the blind necessity of chemistry; renunciation is the only tragic freedom. Beneath the calm classic prose runs a modern dread: that love, like matter, obeys laws we neither choose nor escape.

stops.name: Weimar — the Farbenlehre against Newton
stops.campa: He publishes the Theory of Colours, the labor he prizes above all his poems. Against Newton he denies that white light is a mere bundle of colors; color, he holds, is born at the boundary of light and darkness, the deed and suffering of light, and the eye itself takes part in making it. The physicists reject him; he never yields. Right or wrong in optics, he has seen that the observer and the phenomenon are one act — the whole man, and not mere calculation, meets the world.
stops.quote: Die Farben sind Taten des Lichts, Taten und Leiden.

stops.name: Heidelberg — Marianne von Willemer and the Divan
stops.campa: Aflame with the Persian of Hafiz in Hammer's translation, he answers with the West-Eastern Divan, and in the summer garden of Heidelberg finds his living Suleika in Marianne von Willemer, young wife of a Frankfurt friend. In their veiled play he is Hatem, she Suleika; they exchange poems by the cipher of a shared book, and some of the loveliest verses of the Book of Suleika are hers, not his — the only woman ever to write in his work. They part in September and never meet again.
stops.quote: Und mag die ganze Welt versinken, / Hafis, mit dir, mit dir allein / Will ich wetteifern!

stops.name: Weimar — the death of Christiane
stops.campa: Christiane dies at fifty-one, in convulsions and pain, and Goethe, himself unwell, does not go to the grave in the Jakobsfriedhof; but the night before her death he writes the shaken lines: In vain, thou sun, thou strivest to shine through the gloomy clouds — the whole gain of my life is to weep her loss. Eight-and-twenty years the flower-maker had been the warmth of his house. The town that scorned her he had defied for her; now he mourns in silence, and never again names her aloud.
stops.quote: Du versuchst, o Sonne, vergebens, / Durch die düstren Wolken zu scheinen! / Der ganze Gewinn meines Lebens / Ist, ihren Verlust zu beweinen.
stops.quote_source: On the death of Christiane, June 1816

segments.name: Die letzten Jahre — Marienbad, Eckermann, and More Light (1821–1832)

stops.name: Weimar — Eckermann and the conversations
stops.campa: The young Johann Peter Eckermann comes to Weimar and becomes the Boswell of the sage, walking with him, dining, recording for nine years the old man's talk on art, nature, world-literature, the daemonic and the moment. Through these Conversations the last wisdom of Goethe passes to the world: the counsel to grasp the living whole, to honor the given, to press forward, to make each day serve. Here he coins the very hope of a world-literature, Weltliteratur, wherein the nations shall read one another.
stops.quote: National-Literatur will jetzt nicht viel sagen, die Epoche der Welt-Literatur ist an der Zeit.

stops.name: Marienbad — Ulrike von Levetzow, the last love
stops.campa: At the Bohemian spa of Marienbad the old poet of seventy-four loves the girl Ulrike von Levetzow, not yet nineteen, and in earnest asks for her hand through the Grand Duke himself. Her mother gently refuses. It is the last and most helpless passion of his life. In the swaying coach that carries him away from her toward Weimar he writes, in a week of anguish, the Marienbad Elegy — the naked cry of an old man's renunciation, that he holds among the deepest things he ever made.
stops.quote: Mir ist das All, ich bin mir selbst verloren, / Der ich noch erst den Göttern Liebling war.

stops.name: Weimar — the death of Duke Karl August
stops.campa: Karl August dies, the prince who called him at eighteen and held him fifty-three years — friend, patron, fellow-carouser and fellow-worker, the frame of his whole Weimar life. Grief-stricken, and unable to bear the mourning court, Goethe withdraws to Dornburg above the Saale, among the roses and the vines, and there in the high garden writes his serene late verses to the rising and the setting moon. One by one the companions of his age are going before him; he outlives almost all he loved.

stops.name: Rome — the death of the son August
stops.campa: His only living child, August, sent south for his health and to walk his father's Italian road, dies of smallpox in the night at Rome and is buried near the pyramid of Cestius, by Keats and Shelley's ground. The news reaches the old man at Weimar. He masters himself with the terrible Stoic word — I knew that I begot a mortal — but the shock breaks a blood-vessel; he nearly dies of it. Now he has outlived his son. Only the finishing of Faust holds him to the earth.
stops.quote: Non ignoravi me mortalem genuisse. (Ich wußte, daß ich einen Sterblichen gezeugt hatte.)
suggested_refs: Grave of August von Goethe, Cimitero Acattolico, Rome (Pyramid of Cestius)

stops.name: Weimar — Faust sealed and finished
stops.campa: In his eighty-second year he writes the last lines of Faust, the Second Part — the work begun in his twenties and carried sixty years. Faust, blind at the end, mistakes the digging of his grave for the draining of the marsh, the free people on free soil, and to that vision, not to any pleasure, he says at last the fatal word: linger, thou art so fair — and dies saved, for he has willed the good of others. Goethe seals the manuscript in a packet, to be opened only after his death. His life's labor is complete.
stops.quote: Zum Augenblicke dürft ich sagen: / Verweile doch, du bist so schön! … Im Vorgefühl von solchem hohen Glück / Genieß ich jetzt den höchsten Augenblick.

stops.name: Weimar — the death, 'More Light'
stops.campa: On 22 March, in the house on the Frauenplan, the old man sinks in his armchair, his mind wandering over forms and colors, and asks that the second shutter be opened to let in more light. Toward noon he traces letters in the air upon his knee, a W perhaps, and is still. His last recorded words come down as the great watchword of his life and of his age: More light. The corpse, they say, was of a godlike beauty. The sun that the whole corpus orbited has set; the packet of Faust is opened, and the work goes out to the world.
stops.quote: Mehr Licht!
